claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies cited in the text.

claims.claim: In animals with simultaneous RNAi knockdown of jub and kst, wing size is similar to that of jub RNAi wings.
claims.source: In animals with simultaneous RNAi knockdown of jub and kst, wing size is similar to that of jub RNAi wings (Figure 3B, E–F, and K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The epistasis of jub to kst is consistent with the hypothesis that βH-Spec regulates wing size through its tension-dependent regulation of Jub.
claims.source: The epistasis of jub to kst is consistent with the hypothesis that βH-Spec regulates wing size through its tension-dependent regulation of Jub.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic epistasis data.

claims.claim: Simultaneous RNAi knockdown of Rho kinase (Rok) and βH-Spec reduced wing size and junctional Jub localization similar to that observed in control wing discs with Rok knockdown.
claims.source: To further illustrate this, we reduced tension in wing discs with βH-Spec knockdown by simultaneous RNAi knockdown of Rho kinase (Rok) (Rauskolb et al., 2014; Winter et al., 2001). This reduced wing size and junctional Jub localization similar to that observed in control wing discs with Rok knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Rauskolb et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Knockdown of βH-Spec in posterior compartments caused a mild increase in ex-lacZ expression compared to the anterior compartment and to control posterior compartments.
claims.source: Knockdown of βH-Spec in posterior compartments through the expression of UAS-kst RNAi under en-Gal4 control caused a mild increase in ex-lacZ expression compared to the anterior compartment and to control posterior compartments (Figure 3L and M; Fletcher et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L and M.

claims.claim: Knockdown of jub reduces ex-lacZ expression.
claims.source: Knockdown of jub reduces ex-lacZ expression (Das Thakur et al., 2010; Rauskolb et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies cited in the text.

claims.claim: Simultaneous RNAi knockdown of jub and kst reduced ex-lacZ expression, similar to that in jub RNAi cells.
claims.source: Simultaneous RNAi knockdown of jub and kst reduced ex-lacZ expression, similar to that in jub RNAi cells (Figure 3N and O).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3N and O.

claims.claim: The suppression of the influence of kst on Hippo signaling by jub knockdown is consistent with the inference that βH-Spec regulates Hippo signaling through the Jub biomechanical pathway.
claims.source: The suppression of the influence of kst on Hippo signaling is again consistent with the inference that βH-Spec regulates Hippo signaling through the Jub biomechanical pathway.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic epistasis data.

claims.claim: When α-Spec was knocked down in posterior cells, recruitment of Jub to cell junctions was increased.
claims.source: When α-Spec was knocked down in posterior cells by en-Gal4-driven RNAi, we observed that recruitment of Jub to cell junctions was increased (Figure 2C and F–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and F–H.

claims.claim: The increased wing size and ex-lacZ expression caused by knockdown of α-Spec were suppressed by knockdown of jub.
claims.source: Moreover, as for βH-Spec, we found that the increased wing size and ex-lacZ expression caused by knockdown of α-Spec were suppressed by knockdown of jub (Figure 3G, H, K, P and Q).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: α-Spec regulates Hippo signaling through Jub in wing discs.
claims.source: Thus, as for βH-Spec, and as suggested for pupal eyes (Deng et al., 2020), our observations imply that α-Spec also regulates Hippo signaling through Jub in wing discs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing Jub recruitment and genetic epistasis.

claims.claim: βH-Spec is localized at the apicobasal level of the AJ in wing discs.
claims.source: βH-Spec is localized, as reported previously, at the apicobasal level of the AJ in wing discs (Fletcher et al., 2015; Forest et al., 2018; Figure 4A and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A and C and consistent with previous studies.

claims.claim: α-Spec is enriched in a sub-apical region just below the AJ, with slightly lower levels extending all along the lateral membrane.
claims.source: Conversely, α-Spec is enriched in a sub-apical region just below this, with slightly lower levels extending all along the lateral membrane (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: Only very low levels of α-Spec are detected in the apical plane where βH-Spec is detected, and their distributions in this plane appear to differ.
claims.source: Only very low levels of α-Spec are detected in the apical plane where βH-Spec is detected, and their distributions in this plane appear to differ (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: β-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization.
claims.source: These experiments revealed, as expected, that β-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization (Figure 5B), but it does strongly reduce α-Spec localization (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: β-Spec strongly reduces α-Spec localization.
claims.source: These experiments revealed, as expected, that β-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization (Figure 5B), but it does strongly reduce α-Spec localization (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: α-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization.
claims.source: α-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization (Figure 5A) but its knockdown slightly reduces β-Spec localization (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: α-Spec knockdown slightly reduces β-Spec localization.
claims.source: α-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization (Figure 5A) but its knockdown slightly reduces β-Spec localization (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: βH-Spec depletion does not affect α-Spec localization.
claims.source: Finally, βH-Spec depletion does not affect α-Spec localization (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: While α-Spec needs β-Spec to localize to lateral membranes, the localization of βH-Spec and α-Spec are functionally independent.
claims.source: These observations suggest that while α-Spec needs β-Spec to localize to lateral membranes, the localization of βH-Spec and α-Spec are functionally independent.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi experiments showing independent localization.

claims.claim: A PLA signal consistent with close association of α-Spec and β-Spec was observed in wing discs expressing GFP-tagged β-Spec.
claims.source: A PLA signal consistent with close association of α-Spec and β-Spec was observed in wing discs expressing GFP-tagged β-Spec (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: No significant PLA signal was detected in wing discs expressing GFP-tagged βH-Spec, implying that α-Spec and βH-Spec are not closely associated in wing discs.
claims.source: Conversely, no significant PLA signal was detected in wing discs expressing GFP-tagged βH-Spec, implying that α-Spec and βH-Spec are not closely associated in wing discs (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The distinct localization and PLA results argue against the existence of (αβH)2 complexes in wing imaginal discs.
claims.source: Together with the distinct localization of these proteins revealed by imaging, these observations argue against the existence of (αβH)2 complexes in wing imaginal discs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and PLA data.

claims.claim: The distribution of βH-Spec in wing disc cells appears very similar to the apical distribution of F-actin and myosin.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the distribution of βH-Spec in wing disc cells appears very similar to the apical distribution of F-actin and myosin, and similarities between the localization of βH-Spec and myosin in Drosophila embryos have been noted previously (Krueger et al., 2020; Thomas and Kiehart, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging observations and previous studies.

claims.claim: Kst:GFP and Sqh:mCherry co-localize extensively in the apical region of wing disc epithelial cells.
claims.source: This revealed extensive co-localization between these proteins in the apical region of wing disc epithelial cells (Figure 6A, B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient score between Kst:YFP and Sqh:mCherry was 0.636.
claims.source: Quantitation of these images yielded a Pearson's correlation coefficient score of 0.636.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data.

claims.claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient score between Kst:YFP and α-Spec was 0.18.
claims.source: For comparison, the Pearson's correlation coefficient score between Kst:YFP and α-Spec (Figure 4A) was 0.18.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data.

claims.claim: Kst:GFP and Sqh:mCherry both co-localized with F-actin, with Pearson's correlation coefficient scores of 0.641 and 0.612, respectively.
claims.source: Both Kst:GFP and Sqh:mCherry also co-localized with F-actin, with Pearson's correlation coefficient scores of 0.641 and 0.612, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data.

claims.claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Rok reduces myosin activity by reducing phosphorylation of myosin light chain.
claims.source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Rok reduces myosin activity by reducing phosphorylation of myosin light chain (Winter et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In wing discs, knockdown of Rok is associated with reduced recruitment of myosin to apical junctions and reduced junctional tension.
claims.source: In wing discs, knockdown of Rok is also associated with reduced recruitment of myosin to apical junctions and reduced junctional tension (Rauskolb et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the generally positive correlation between myosin activity and co-localization with F-actin (Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Noll et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and previous studies.

claims.claim: Examination of βH-Spec in wing disc cells expressing Rok RNAi revealed increased levels of βH-Spec along apical junctions.
claims.source: Conversely, examination of βH-Spec in wing disc cells expressing Rok RNAi revealed increased levels of βH-Spec along apical junctions (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Expression of constitutively activated, phosphomimetic form of myosin light chain (SqhEE) increases the recruitment of myosin to AJ and increases junctional tension.
claims.source: This increases the recruitment of myosin to AJ and increases junctional tension (Rauskolb et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), but decreases the recruitment of βH-Spec to AJ, and a portion of βH-Spec instead appears in apical vesicles (Figure 6E, F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and previous studies.

claims.claim: Expression of SqhEE decreases the recruitment of βH-Spec to AJ, and a portion of βH-Spec instead appears in apical vesicles.
claims.source: This increases the recruitment of myosin to AJ and increases junctional tension (Rauskolb et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), but decreases the recruitment of βH-Spec to AJ, and a portion of βH-Spec instead appears in apical vesicles (Figure 6E, F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claims.claim: Myosin antagonizes localization of βH-Spec to AJ.
claims.source: Calculation of the ratio of intensities of the anterior (control) versus posterior (experimental) compartments further confirmed our observation that myosin antagonizes localization of βH-Spec to AJ (Figure 6G–J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 6G–J.

claims.claim: βH-Spec and myosin II localization to AJ are affected in opposite ways by changes in cytoskeletal tension.
claims.source: Thus, βH-Spec and myosin II localization to AJ are affected in opposite ways by changes in cytoskeletal tension.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing opposite effects of tension manipulation.

claims.claim: Overexpression of βH-Spec using a CRISPR-activator (CRISPRa) approach effectively increased expression of Kst:GFP.
claims.source: Both imaging and western blotting of wing discs confirmed that this CRISPRa approach effectively increased expression of Kst:GFP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B.

claims.claim: Examination of myosin under βH-Spec overexpression conditions revealed a substantial reduction of myosin localization to AJs.
claims.source: Examination of myosin under βH-Spec overexpression conditions, using Sqh:GFP, revealed a substantial reduction of myosin localization to AJs (Figure 7A, C and E–F), and a reduction in tension along cell junctions as assayed by the recoil speed after laser cutting (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: βH-Spec overexpression reduced tension along cell junctions as assayed by the recoil speed after laser cutting.
claims.source: Examination of myosin under βH-Spec overexpression conditions, using Sqh:GFP, revealed a substantial reduction of myosin localization to AJs (Figure 7A, C and E–F), and a reduction in tension along cell junctions as assayed by the recoil speed after laser cutting (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I.

claims.claim: Apical cell areas were increased under βH-Spec overexpression conditions, consistent with a reduction of junctional tension.
claims.source: Apical cell areas were also increased, consistent with a reduction of junctional tension (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Overexpression of βH-Spec using UAS-kstEP under en-Gal4 control reduced myosin levels at AJ.
claims.source: Overexpression of βH-Spec using UAS-kstEP under en-Gal4 control also reduced myosin levels at AJ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), although the effect appeared weaker than that induced by the CRISPRa approach.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: βH-Spec antagonizes myosin recruitment to AJs under both increased and decreased βH-Spec expression conditions.
claims.source: These results provide further evidence that βH-Spec antagonizes myosin recruitment to AJs and establish that this effect can be observed under both increased and decreased βH-Spec expression conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from both knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: βH-Spec overexpression reduced junctional recruitment of Jub.
claims.source: Consistent with these reductions in apical myosin accumulation, βH-Spec overexpression also reduced junctional recruitment of Jub (Figure 7B, D, G, and H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) and decreased wing size (wings were 92% and 89% of nub-Gal4 UAS-dcr2 control size, for the two different overexpression constructs) (Figure 3I–K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: βH-Spec overexpression decreased wing size (wings were 92% and 89% of nub-Gal4 UAS-dcr2 control size, for the two different overexpression constructs).
claims.source: Consistent with these reductions in apical myosin accumulation, βH-Spec overexpression also reduced junctional recruitment of Jub (Figure 7B, D, G, and H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) and decreased wing size (wings were 92% and 89% of nub-Gal4 UAS-dcr2 control size, for the two different overexpression constructs) (Figure 3I–K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I–K.

claims.claim: βH-Spec contains two N-terminal actin-binding domains, CH1 and CH2.
claims.source: βH-Spec contains two N-terminal actin-binding domains, CH1 and CH2 (Liem, 2016), and myosin contains an actin-binding region in its motor domain (Duan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Myosin contains an actin-binding region in its motor domain.
claims.source: βH-Spec contains two N-terminal actin-binding domains, CH1 and CH2 (Liem, 2016), and myosin contains an actin-binding region in its motor domain (Duan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The isolated Drosophila βH-Spec actin-binding region binds F-actin weakly.
claims.source: We found that the isolated Drosophila βH-Spec actin-binding region binds F-actin weakly (Figure 8A), in agreement with previous reports of F-actin binding by other spectrin CH1-CH2 domains (Avery et al., 2017; Duan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 8A and consistent with previous studies.

claims.claim: Constitutively active Drosophila myosin II binding to F-actin appears stronger than βH-Spec binding.
claims.source: Constitutively active Drosophila myosin II (subfragment-1-like protein) binding to F-actin appears stronger than βH-Spec binding, as at the same concentration a greater fraction of myosin II is bound to F-actin (Figure 8A, B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claims.claim: Myosin can displace the actin-binding region of βH-Spec from F-actin by ~50% at the highest myosin concentration tested.
claims.source: We found that myosin can displace the actin-binding region of βH-Spec from F-actin by ~50% at the highest myosin concentration that we could use (Figure 8C, bottom right).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro competition assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Myosin binding to F-actin was unaffected by preincubation with βH-Spec CH domains, likely due to active myosin's higher binding affinity for F-actin.
claims.source: Myosin binding to F-actin was unaffected by preincubation with βH-Spec CH domains (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), likely due to active myosin's higher binding affinity for F-actin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro competition assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, with an inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: The binding position of the CH1 domain on F-actin sterically interferes with the formation of a strong actin-myosin interface.
claims.source: The superimposition of both models suggests that the binding position of the CH1 domain on F-actin sterically interferes with the formation of a strong actin-myosin interface (Figure 8D'').
claims.evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 8D''.

claims.claim: Modeling of the βH-Spec CH1-CH2 domain indicates that the CH2 domain presents additional steric hindrance for myosin binding to F-actin.
claims.source: Modeling of the βH-Spec CH1-CH2 domain indicates that the CH2 domain presents additional steric hindrance for myosin binding to F-actin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–B'').
claims.evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–B''.

claims.claim: Structural modeling suggests that the binding of spectrin or myosin to individual binding sites on F-actin is mutually exclusive.
claims.source: Thus, structural modeling suggests that the binding of spectrin or myosin to individual binding sites on F-actin is mutually exclusive, which could explain why they compete for F-actin association in vivo and in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling data.

claims.claim: When βH-Spec or α-Spec levels are decreased by RNAi, levels of junctional myosin are increased.
claims.source: In contrast to prior studies, we observed that when βH-Spec or α-Spec levels are decreased by RNAi, levels of junctional myosin are increased.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: The increase in junctional myosin levels caused by spectrin knockdown is associated with increased junctional tension and with increased recruitment of Jub to AJ.
claims.source: This increase in junctional myosin levels is associated with increased junctional tension and with increased recruitment of Jub to AJ.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased tension and Jub recruitment.

claims.claim: jub is genetically required for the influence of spectrin knockdown on Yki activity and wing growth.
claims.source: Moreover, our results are further supported by the observation that jub is genetically required for the influence of spectrin knockdown on Yki activity and wing growth.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis experiments showing suppression of spectrin knockdown phenotypes by jub knockdown.

claims.claim: βH-Spec and α-Spec regulate Hippo signaling in wing discs through the Jub biomechanical pathway.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations imply that βH-Spec and α-Spec regulate Hippo signaling in wing discs through the Jub biomechanical pathway, rather than through hypothesized alternate mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing Jub recruitment and genetic epistasis.

claims.claim: βH-Spec functions independently of α-Spec in wing imaginal discs.
claims.source: However, our observations indicate that βH-Spec functions independently of α-Spec in wing imaginal discs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on localization and functional data.

claims.claim: α-Spec and βH-Spec do not exhibit significant co-localization.
claims.source: α-Spec and βH-Spec do not exhibit significant co-localization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing distinct localization patterns.

claims.claim: α-Spec and βH-Spec are not required for each other's localization to apical cell junctions.
claims.source: Moreover, α-Spec and βH-Spec are not required for each other's localization to apical cell junctions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing independent localization.

claims.claim: β-Spec is required for recruitment of α-Spec to lateral membranes in wing discs.
claims.source: This contrasts with the requirement for β-Spec for recruitment of α-Spec to lateral membranes in wing discs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing that β-Spec knockdown reduces α-Spec localization.

claims.claim: β-Spec subunits have a pleckstrin homology domain that can mediate membrane association, as well as possessing the CH domains that mediate F-actin association.
claims.source: β-Spec subunits, but not α-Spec subunits, have a pleckstrin homology domain that can mediate membrane association, as well as possessing the CH domains that mediate F-actin association.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about spectrin domain structure.

claims.claim: β-Spec can associate with lateral membranes without α-Spec, but α-Spec does not have a way to associate with lateral membranes without β-Spec.
claims.source: Thus β-Spec can associate with lateral membranes without α-Spec, but α-Spec does not have a way to associate with lateral membranes without β-Spec.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the domain structure and localization data.

claims.claim: An independent role for βH-Spec has been suggested in mammalian photoreceptors, where mammalian βV-Spec does not co-localize with αII-spectrin.
claims.source: An independent role for βH-Spec has also been suggested in mammalian photoreceptors, where it was reported that that mammalian βV-Spec does not co-localize with αII-spectrin, and that βV-Spec could form homodimers, potentially allowing it to cross-link actin by itself, enabling α-Spec-independent functions (Papal et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claims.claim: The results do not exclude the possibility that βH-Spec and α-Spec might act together in a physical complex in other tissues, or under distinct physiological conditions.
claims.source: Nonetheless, our results do not exclude the possibility that βH-Spec and α-Spec might act together in a physical complex in other tissues, or under distinct physiological conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about potential alternative scenarios.

claims.claim: βH-Spec and α-Spec act independently in wing discs, implying that they influence tension at apical junctions through distinct mechanisms.
claims.source: The conclusion that βH-Spec and α-Spec act independently in wing discs implies that they influence tension at apical junctions through distinct mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the independent localization and function data.

claims.claim: α-Spec could influence AJ tension in wing discs through the mechanism proposed for pupal eyes, where α- and β-Spec maintain cell rigidity by linking F-actin to membranes.
claims.source: We suggest that α-Spec could influence AJ tension in wing discs through the mechanism proposed to explain the influence of α- and β-Spec in pupal eyes (Deng et al., 2020). It was inferred that α- and β-Spec maintain cell rigidity by linking F-actin to membranes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on a previous study and the observed phenotypes.

claims.claim: In the absence of α- or β-Spec, dissociation between F-actin and the membrane leads to an expansion of the apical regions, which increases cytoskeletal tension at AJs.
claims.source: In the absence of α- or β-Spec, it was proposed that dissociation between F-actin and the membrane leads to an expansion of the apical regions. This expansion increases cytoskeletal tension at AJs, which bind F-actin independently of spectrins.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from a previous study.

claims.claim: A decrease in cell height was observed in α-Spec knockdown cells in wing discs, in conjunction with increased tension at apical junctions.
claims.source: Consistent with this suggested mechanism, we observed a decrease in cell height in α-Spec knockdown cells in wing discs, in conjunction with increased tension at apical junctions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced epithelial thickness and increased tension.

claims.claim: The alteration in cell shape was not observed in βH-Spec knockdown cells, supporting the conclusion that βH-Spec and α-Spec act in different ways to regulate junctional tension.
claims.source: The alteration in cell shape was not observed in βH-Spec knockdown cells, further supporting the conclusion that βH-Spec and α-Spec act in different ways to regulate junctional tension.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no change in epithelial thickness with βH-Spec knockdown.

claims.claim: A mutual antagonism exists between βH-Spec and myosin in vivo for localization to apical F-actin.
claims.source: We observed a mutual antagonism between βH-Spec and myosin in vivo for localization to apical F-actin: decreasing βH-Spec increases junctional myosin, while increasing βH-Spec decreases junctional myosin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from both knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: Increasing myosin activity decreases βH-Spec localization to apical F-actin, while decreasing myosin activity increases βH-Spec localization to apical F-actin.
claims.source: Reciprocally, increasing myosin activity decreases βH-Spec localization to apical F-actin, while decreasing myosin activity increases βH-Spec localization to apical F-actin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data using SqhEE and Rok RNAi.

claims.claim: In vitro studies with purified protein domains revealed that myosin can compete with βH-Spec for binding to F-actin.
claims.source: In vitro studies with purified protein domains revealed that myosin can compete with βH-Spec for binding to F-actin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-sedimentation assay data.

claims.claim: Computational modeling of protein structures revealed that myosin and βH-Spec would interfere with each other's binding to F-actin.
claims.source: Finally, computational modeling of protein structures revealed that myosin and βH-Spec would interfere with each other's binding to F-actin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural modeling data.

claims.claim: βH-Spec and myosin can directly compete with each other for localization to F-actin.
claims.source: Together, these observations indicate that βH-Spec and myosin can directly compete with each other for localization to F-actin.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo, in vitro, and modeling data.

claims.claim: The influence of βH-Spec on junctional tension is likely to be a direct consequence of its competition with myosin for overlapping binding sites on F-actin.
claims.source: We suggest therefore that the influence of βH-Spec on junctional tension is likely to be a direct consequence of its competition with myosin for overlapping binding sites on F-actin.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the competition data and the observed effects on tension.

claims.claim: The CH2 domain regulates the actin binding function of the CH1 domain through steric hindrance when the two domains are associated.
claims.source: Second, it has been suggested for β-Spec that the CH2 domain regulates the actin binding function of the CH1 domain through steric hindrance when the two domains are associated (Avery et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claims.claim: A specific mutation in β-Spec CH2 (L253P) has been shown to lower the energetic barrier between closed and open structural states, increasing the affinity of β-Spec for F-actin around 1000-fold.
claims.source: A specific mutation in β-Spec CH2 (L253P) has been shown to lower the energetic barrier between closed and open structural states, increasing the affinity of β-Spec for F-actin around 1000-fold (Avery et al., 2016), but it is unknown how β-Spec or βH-Spec conformational changes are normally regulated in vivo and whether both proteins share this regulatory feature.
claims.evidence: This is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain shifts myosin from a compact, autoinhibited conformation to a filamentous, active conformation.
claims.source: Additionally, phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain shifts myosin from a compact, autoinhibited conformation to a filamentous, active conformation (Kiehart and Feghali, 1986; Vasquez et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The autoinhibited conformation of myosin binds F-actin very weakly (KD>100 µM) compared to the active conformation.
claims.source: The autoinhibited conformation binds F-actin very weakly (KD>100 µM) (Heissler and Manstein, 2013; Sellers et al., 1982) compared to the active conformation, suggesting that spectrin could outcompete autoinhibited myosin more effectively than active myosin for binding to F-actin.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The competition between βH-Spec and myosin provides key insights into how βH-Spec contributes to ratcheting of apical constriction.
claims.source: The competition between βH-Spec and myosin also provides key insights into how βH-Spec contributes to ratcheting of apical constriction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the competition model and knowledge of ratcheting mechanisms.

claims.claim: The apical constriction of cells in the ventral furrow that initiates Drosophila mesoderm invagination occurs through fast constriction pulses interrupted by pauses during which cells must stabilize their constricted state before reinitiating constriction.
claims.source: The apical constriction of cells in the ventral furrow that initiates Drosophila mesoderm invagination occurs through fast constriction pulses interrupted by pauses during which cells must stabilize their constricted state before reinitiating constriction (Martin et al., 2009; Xie and Martin, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Ratcheting-like behavior during apical constriction is thought to be a consequence of the finite length of actin filaments.
claims.source: This ratcheting-like behavior is thought to be a consequence of the finite length of actin filaments.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ratcheting mechanisms.

claims.claim: Myosin contracts the cytoskeleton by driving filaments past each other, and extensive contractions require release and reassociation with new pairs of filaments.
claims.source: Myosin contracts the cytoskeleton by driving filaments past each other, and extensive contractions require release and reassociation with new pairs of filaments.

results.result: βH-Spec and α-Spec knockdown increases junctional myosin levels, junctional tension, and Jub recruitment to adherens junctions in wing imaginal discs.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 provide experimental evidence showing increased pMLC, myosin levels, and junctional tension upon spectrin knockdown. Claim C40 demonstrates increased Jub recruitment. These findings are internally consistent and supported by multiple independent measurements (imaging, laser ablation, quantification), contradicting prior reports (C32) but aligning with established tension-Jub relationships (C39).

results.result: βH-Spec and α-Spec regulate Hippo signaling through the Jub biomechanical pathway, as demonstrated by genetic epistasis experiments showing jub knockdown suppresses spectrin knockdown phenotypes on wing size and ex-lacZ expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C49 present genetic epistasis data showing that jub knockdown suppresses the effects of spectrin knockdown on both wing size and Hippo pathway reporter expression. The epistasis is consistent across multiple readouts and with tension manipulation experiments (C45), providing strong evidence for the Jub-dependent mechanism. Statistical significance is reported (Figure 3K).

results.result: α-Spec regulates Hippo signaling through Jub in wing discs, similar to βH-Spec.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 provide experimental evidence that α-Spec knockdown increases Jub recruitment and that jub knockdown suppresses α-Spec knockdown phenotypes. This parallels the findings for βH-Spec and is supported by imaging and genetic data, though the authors note this differs from previous interpretations (C28-C29).

results.result: βH-Spec localizes and functions independently of α-Spec in wing imaginal discs, as shown by distinct subcellular localization patterns, lack of proximity ligation signal, and independent localization in RNAi experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 show distinct localization patterns by imaging (Pearson correlation 0.18). Claims C58-C60 demonstrate through RNAi that neither spectrin requires the other for apical localization. Claim C63 shows no PLA signal between α-Spec and βH-Spec, while C62 shows positive PLA for α-Spec and β-Spec. These multiple independent lines of evidence strongly support independent function.

results.result: β-Spec is required for α-Spec localization to lateral membranes but not vice versa, consistent with β-Spec having membrane-binding domains that α-Spec lacks.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 show through RNAi that β-Spec knockdown strongly reduces α-Spec localization while β-Spec localization is independent of βH-Spec. Claims C102-C103 provide a mechanistic explanation based on domain structure (pleckstrin homology domain in β-Spec). This is consistent with established knowledge and the experimental data.

results.result: βH-Spec and myosin II extensively co-localize at the apical region of wing disc cells, with a Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.636.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 provide quantitative co-localization data from imaging experiments. The Pearson's correlation of 0.636 between Kst:GFP and Sqh:mCherry is substantially higher than the 0.18 correlation between Kst:YFP and α-Spec, supporting extensive co-localization. Both proteins also co-localize with F-actin with similar correlation coefficients (~0.64 and 0.61).

results.result: βH-Spec and myosin reciprocally antagonize each other's localization to apical junctions: reducing myosin activity increases βH-Spec localization while increasing myosin activity decreases βH-Spec localization, and vice versa.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 show that Rok RNAi (reducing myosin) increases βH-Spec at junctions while SqhEE (increasing myosin) decreases βH-Spec. Claims C36-C37 and C78-C81 show the reciprocal effect. The data include imaging, quantification, and heat maps. The reciprocal nature is demonstrated in both directions with appropriate controls.

results.result: Overexpression of βH-Spec reduces myosin localization to adherens junctions, decreases junctional tension, reduces Jub recruitment, and decreases wing size.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C84 present data from two independent overexpression methods (CRISPRa and EP element). Both show reduced myosin at junctions, decreased tension (laser ablation), reduced Jub recruitment, and smaller wings (92% and 89% of control). The consistency across methods and multiple readouts provides strong support.

results.result: βH-Spec and myosin compete for binding to F-actin in vitro, with myosin displacing approximately 50% of βH-Spec from F-actin at the highest concentration tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C90 present in vitro co-sedimentation data showing weak βH-Spec binding to F-actin, stronger myosin binding, and ~50% displacement of βH-Spec by myosin. However, C90 notes that myosin binding was unaffected by pre-incubation with βH-Spec, indicating asymmetric competition. The authors acknowledge experimental limitations (protein concentration constraints). The data support competition but with caveats about the in vitro conditions.

results.result: Structural modeling indicates that βH-Spec CH domains and myosin have overlapping binding sites on F-actin, with the CH1 domain sterically interfering with myosin binding and CH2 providing additional steric hindrance.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 describe structural modeling showing overlapping binding sites on F-actin subdomains SD1-SD3. The modeling is based on established structures (human β-III spectrin, myosin) and homology modeling for Drosophila proteins. While modeling has inherent uncertainties, the approach is appropriate and the conclusions about steric interference are reasonable given the structural data.

results.result: The competition between βH-Spec and myosin for F-actin binding explains βH-Spec's influence on cytoskeletal tension and myosin accumulation.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic interpretation (C7, C117) is well-supported by the convergence of in vivo reciprocal antagonism data (C112-C113), in vitro competition assays (C89), and structural modeling (C91-C93). The model provides a parsimonious explanation for the observed phenotypes, though the authors appropriately note it as a suggested mechanism rather than definitively proven.

results.result: The competition between βH-Spec and myosin provides insight into βH-Spec's role in ratcheting mechanisms during apical constriction, where myosin release naturally couples to βH-Spec binding for stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 cite established knowledge about βH-Spec's role in ratcheting. Claims C129-C131 present a mechanistic model where competition naturally coordinates myosin-mediated contraction with βH-Spec-mediated stabilization. This is a logical inference from the competition data, though it remains a proposed mechanism rather than directly tested. The model addresses a previously unexplained coordination problem.

results.result: α-Spec and βH-Spec regulate junctional tension through distinct mechanisms, with α-Spec affecting epithelial thickness (reduced by knockdown) while βH-Spec does not, suggesting α-Spec acts by linking F-actin to membranes.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 provides experimental data showing differential effects on epithelial thickness. Claims C108-C111 propose a mechanism based on prior work in pupal eyes and the observed phenotypes. The differential effect on cell shape supports distinct mechanisms, though the proposed mechanism for α-Spec is more speculative and based largely on analogy to other systems.

results.result: Prior studies reported that spectrin knockdown increased myosin activity (pMLC) but surprisingly did not affect myosin or F-actin levels, which contradicts the general correlation between myosin activity and accumulation.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately represent prior literature (C31-C32 cite Deng et al., 2015) and note the contradiction with established principles (C33). This provides important context for the current study's findings that do show increased myosin levels. The claims are about prior work rather than new findings.

results.result: Proximity ligation assay shows close association between α-Spec and β-Spec but not between α-Spec and βH-Spec in wing discs.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 present PLA data showing positive signal for α-Spec/β-Spec but not for α-Spec/βH-Spec. This biochemical evidence complements the localization data. However, PLA has distance limitations (~40 nm) and negative results should be interpreted cautiously. The positive control (α-Spec/β-Spec) validates the approach.

results.result: Conformational regulation may affect spectrin and myosin binding to F-actin, with CH2 domain regulating CH1 binding in β-Spec and phosphorylation shifting myosin between autoinhibited and active conformations.
results.evaluation: These claims (C118-C121) cite established literature about conformational regulation of spectrin and myosin. They provide context for interpreting the in vitro competition results and explain why spectrin might compete more effectively with inactive myosin. These are background knowledge claims rather than new findings.

results.result: Spectrin depletion increases myosin levels, junctional tension, and pMLC. Knockdown of βH-Spec or α-Spec in wing disc cells led to increased apical myosin accumulation, increased phosphorylated myosin light chain (pMLC), and increased junctional tension as measured by laser cutting recoil velocity. However, α-Spec and βH-Spec knockdown differed in that epithelial thickness was reduced by α-Spec knockdown but not by βH-Spec knockdown.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge these findings, with one reviewer stating that 'contrary to previous reports, the authors reveal that, indeed, depletion of alpha- and beta-heavy-spectrin leads to an increase in myosin levels at the apical membrane.' The data are described as 'compelling' and the experimental approach is praised for its tissue specificity and quantitative methods.

results.result: Spectrin depletion increases Jub recruitment to adherens junctions. The increased junctional tension and myosin activity caused by βH-Spec or α-Spec depletion is associated with increased junctional recruitment of Jub, as visualized by Jub:GFP localization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly confirm this finding, with one stating 'the authors also reveal that the depletion of spectrins leads to an increase in Ajuba levels.' This directly contradicts previous reports and is treated as a key finding that reconciles conflicting literature. The reviewers note the data are 'compelling' and the conclusions 'supported by the presented data.'

results.result: Spectrins regulate Hippo signaling and wing growth through the Jub biomechanical pathway. Genetic epistasis experiments show that jub knockdown suppresses the effects of βH-Spec or α-Spec knockdown on wing size and ex-lacZ expression (a Hippo pathway readout), indicating that spectrins act through Jub to regulate Hippo signaling and organ size.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this conclusion, stating 'the data are compelling in establishing that alpha and beta spectrin regulate the Hippo signaling pathway independently via their effect on cytoskeletal tension.' The genetic epistasis analysis is specifically praised as a strength of the study, and reviewers note that 'the author's conclusions are supported by the presented data.'

results.result: βH-spectrin localizes and functions independently of α-spectrin in wing discs. Imaging shows distinct localization patterns for βH-Spec (apical at AJ level) and α-Spec (sub-apical/lateral), with minimal co-localization. RNAi experiments demonstrate that βH-Spec and α-Spec localization are independent of each other. Proximity ligation assay (PLA) shows no significant signal between α-Spec and βH-Spec, arguing against (αβH)2 complexes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding as a major contribution, stating 'Against the classical view, the work shows that βH-Spec can act independently of α-Spec.' One reviewer notes this is 'unexpected' and that 'the authors conclude that βH-Spec and α-Spec act independently in this regulation.' The localization and functional independence data are treated as well-supported by the reviewers.

results.result: βH-spectrin co-localizes extensively with myosin at apical junctions. Imaging of Kst:GFP and Sqh:mCherry shows extensive co-localization in the apical region with a Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.636, much higher than the correlation between Kst:YFP and α-Spec (0.18). Both proteins also co-localize with F-actin.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about the co-localization data. One reviewer notes 'the method of quantifying protein localization and abundance is common for multiple figures which makes it easy to assess differences across experiments,' implicitly accepting the quantitative co-localization measurements. The finding is treated as supporting the competition model.

results.result: βH-spectrin and myosin reciprocally regulate each other's localization. Reducing myosin activity (Rok RNAi) increases βH-Spec at junctions, while increasing myosin activity (SqhEE expression) decreases βH-Spec at junctions. Conversely, βH-Spec depletion increases myosin levels and βH-Spec overexpression decreases myosin levels at adherens junctions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this reciprocal relationship, with one stating 'the major point of this study is that the apical localization of βH-Spec and myosin is mutually exclusive and that the proteins antagonize each other's activity in wing discs.' The reviewers describe the flow of experiments as 'logical' and state that 'the author's conclusions are supported by the presented data.'

results.result: βH-spectrin overexpression reduces myosin, tension, Jub recruitment, and wing size. Using CRISPR-activation to overexpress βH-Spec resulted in reduced myosin localization to AJs, reduced junctional tension (measured by laser cutting), reduced Jub recruitment, increased apical cell areas, and decreased wing size.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praise the 'elegant CRISPR-based overexpression system with great tissue specificity' as a strength of the study. The reciprocal effects of overexpression compared to knockdown are treated as supporting the competition model. No concerns are raised about these complementary gain-of-function experiments.

results.result: βH-spectrin and myosin directly compete for F-actin binding. In vitro co-sedimentation assays show that both βH-Spec CH domains and myosin bind F-actin, with myosin having stronger binding. Myosin can displace βH-Spec from F-actin by ~50%. Structural modeling indicates that the binding sites overlap and are mutually exclusive, providing a molecular mechanism for the competition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this mechanism, stating 'In vitro co-sedimentation assays and in silico structural modeling suggest that this antagonization is due to a competition of βH-Spec and myosin for F-actin binding.' One reviewer notes 'The molecular mechanism regulating myosin activity by out-competing it for F-actin binding has been observed for small actin-binding proteins such as cofilin but is a new mode for such a big, membrane-associated actin-binding protein.'

results.result: Competition between βH-spectrin and myosin explains spectrin's influence on cytoskeletal tension and provides insight into ratcheting mechanisms. The direct competition for F-actin binding explains how βH-Spec influences cytoskeletal tension and myosin accumulation. This competition model provides a mechanism for how myosin-mediated contraction can alternate with βH-Spec-mediated stabilization during ratcheting of apical constriction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these mechanistic interpretations, with one stating 'the antagonistic activity of βH-Spec and myosin in this tissue context might help explain phenomena in other systems such as spectrin-dependent ratcheting of apical constriction during mesoderm invagination (as the authors discuss).' The reviewers treat the competition model as well-supported and note it 'will be of interest to the cell biology community.'

results.result: β-spectrin is required for α-spectrin localization to lateral membranes but not for βH-spectrin localization. RNAi experiments show that β-Spec knockdown strongly reduces α-Spec localization but does not affect βH-Spec localization. PLA shows close association between α-Spec and β-Spec. This indicates that α-Spec requires β-Spec for lateral membrane localization, consistent with (αβ)2 tetramers at lateral membranes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these localization dependencies. The findings are treated as consistent with the overall model of independent βH-Spec function and are implicitly accepted as part of the well-supported localization analysis that reviewers praise for its quantitative approach.

results.result: α-spectrin and βH-spectrin regulate junctional tension through distinct mechanisms. The independent action of βH-Spec and α-Spec implies distinct mechanisms. α-Spec may act by linking F-actin to membranes to maintain cell rigidity, with loss leading to apical expansion and increased AJ tension (consistent with reduced cell height observed). βH-Spec acts through direct competition with myosin for F-actin binding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the distinct mechanisms, noting that the work establishes 'alpha and beta spectrin regulate the Hippo signaling pathway independently.' The differential effects on cell shape (epithelial thickness) are treated as supporting evidence for distinct mechanisms. No concerns are raised about this interpretation.

results.result: Reducing tension by Rok knockdown suppresses the effects of βH-Spec depletion. Simultaneous knockdown of Rok and βH-Spec reduced wing size and Jub localization similar to Rok knockdown alone, demonstrating that the effects of βH-Spec depletion depend on increased tension.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about this epistasis experiment. It is treated as part of the logical flow of experiments that support the tension-dependent mechanism. The reviewers note 'the flow of experiments is logical' and the conclusions are supported.

results.result: Structural modeling indicates steric interference between βH-spectrin and myosin binding to F-actin. Modeling shows that the CH1 domain binding position sterically interferes with myosin binding, and the CH2 domain presents additional steric hindrance. The binding is predicted to be mutually exclusive at individual F-actin binding sites.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge the structural modeling as supporting the competition mechanism, stating 'in silico structural modeling suggest that this antagonization is due to a competition of βH-Spec and myosin for F-actin binding.' No concerns are raised about the modeling approach or conclusions.

comparisons.comparison: Strong agreement on independent function of βH-Spec and α-Spec (C3, C53-C55, C58-C64, C98-C100). Both evaluations treat the localization data, RNAi experiments, and PLA results as compelling evidence for this major finding that challenges classical views. Jaccard index: 0.923.

Strong agreement on reciprocal antagonism between βH-Spec and myosin (C5, C72-C76, C112-C113). Both evaluations affirm the mutual exclusivity and reciprocal regulation as well-supported by the data. Peer reviewers describe the experimental flow as 'logical.' Jaccard index: 0.875.

Strong agreement on co-localization of βH-Spec with myosin and F-actin (C4, C66-C69). Both evaluations accept the quantitative Pearson correlation data. Peer reviewers implicitly endorse the measurements by praising the quantification methods. Jaccard index: 0.833.

Strong agreement on distinct mechanisms for α-Spec and βH-Spec (C107-C111). Both evaluations accept the differential effects on epithelial thickness and the proposed mechanistic explanations, though OpenEval notes the α-Spec mechanism is more speculative. Jaccard index: 0.833.

Strong agreement on βH-Spec overexpression effects (C78-C84). Both evaluations praise the CRISPR-based overexpression approach and accept the reciprocal effects on myosin, tension, Jub recruitment, and wing size as supporting the competition model. Jaccard index: 0.75.

Strong agreement on genetic epistasis showing Jub-dependent mechanism (C41-C49, C96-C97). Both evaluations affirm that jub knockdown suppresses spectrin knockdown effects on wing size and Hippo signaling. Peer reviewers specifically praise the epistasis analysis. Jaccard index: 0.667.

Strong agreement on competition mechanism from in vitro and modeling data (C6, C87-C89, C114-C117). Both evaluations accept the co-sedimentation assays and structural modeling as supporting F-actin competition. OpenEval notes experimental limitations while peer reviewers highlight novelty of the mechanism. Jaccard index: 0.667.

Strong agreement on structural modeling showing overlapping binding sites (C91-C93). Both evaluations accept the modeling approach and conclusions about steric interference. No concerns raised by either evaluation. Jaccard index: 0.6.

Strong agreement on increased myosin and tension upon spectrin knockdown (C34-C37). Both evaluations explicitly note this contradicts previous reports and treat the data as 'compelling.' Peer reviewers praise tissue specificity and quantitative methods. OpenEval also addresses C40, C94-C95 not covered in this peer result. Jaccard index: 0.444.

Strong agreement on mechanistic model for coordination of contraction and stabilization (C8, C122, C130-C131). Both evaluations support the proposed mechanism linking competition to ratcheting phenomena. Peer reviewers note relevance to other systems. OpenEval also addresses C126-C129. Jaccard index: 0.364.

Strong agreement on β-Spec dependence for α-Spec localization (C56-C57, C101). Both evaluations accept the RNAi data showing asymmetric dependence. OpenEval additionally addresses mechanistic explanation (C102-C103) not explicitly covered in peer result. Jaccard index: 0.333.

Both address increased Jub recruitment upon spectrin knockdown (C40, C95). OpenEval groups this with myosin/tension data (R1), while peer reviewers treat it as a separate key finding (R2) that reconciles conflicting literature. Both strongly support the finding. Jaccard index: 0.222.

Partial overlap on α-Spec effects (C50-C51). OpenEval addresses α-Spec increasing Jub recruitment and epistasis with jub knockdown. Peer R2 focuses on broader epistasis analysis including α-Spec. Both support the findings. Jaccard index: 0.2.

Minimal overlap (C51 only). OpenEval R3 addresses α-Spec effects on Jub and phenotypes. Peer R3 focuses on broader epistasis analysis. Both support Jub-dependent regulation but address different aspects. Jaccard index: 0.091.

Minimal overlap (C45 only). OpenEval R2 addresses broad epistasis analysis including tension manipulation. Peer R12 specifically addresses this tension manipulation experiment. Both support the findings. Jaccard index: 0.091.

Minimal overlap on PLA data (C63). OpenEval R15 specifically evaluates PLA experiments with methodological caveats. Peer R4 addresses broader independent function evidence including PLA. Both support the findings. Jaccard index: 0.077.

Minimal overlap (C7 only). OpenEval R11 addresses mechanistic interpretation of competition model. Peer R9 addresses broader mechanistic implications including ratcheting. Both strongly support the competition mechanism. Jaccard index: 0.125.
